title: Essay titles for revision
description: Three essay titles from this week’s lectures. Note them down for revision, and write any of them here for practice.
instructions:
Optional, for revision. These are essay titles that go with this week’s lectures. It’s worth noting them down, as they’re good practice for the exam. Only the practical question and the two short-answer questions need to be handed in.

  • You can write any of them here for practice, as you would in the exam: about 40 minutes each, without notes. You don’t need to answer all of them.
  • Planning an answer to each one (your argument, your evidence and the order you’d put them in) is good revision too.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the ground each title covers.

questions.title: Sodium and the action potential
questions.text: What is the evidence for the involvement of sodium ions in the nerve action potential?
questions.guidance:
Some points to consider. This isn’t a model answer.

  • The overshoot. When Hodgkin and Huxley first recorded from inside a squid giant axon (1939), the action potential didn’t just cancel the resting potential but overshot zero. A membrane simply losing its selectivity can’t explain that, but a rise in its permeability to an ion with a positive equilibrium potential can, and Na+ is the obvious candidate.
  • Changing the Na+ outside. Overton (1902) found that frog muscle stopped responding in a solution without Na+. Hodgkin and Katz (1949) showed that lowering the Na+ outside a squid axon lowered the peak of the action potential and slowed its rise, by close to the 58 mV per tenfold change that the Nernst equation predicts for Na+.
  • The voltage clamp. Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) held the membrane potential steady and measured the currents. The early inward current reversed near ENa and disappeared when the Na+ outside was replaced, while the later outward current was carried by K+. A model built from these conductances reproduced the action potential’s shape and its speed of conduction.
  • Tracers. Radioactive sodium showed a small extra influx of Na+ with each impulse (Keynes, 1951).
  • Blockers and channels. Tetrodotoxin blocks the early inward current and the action potential (Narahashi and colleagues, 1964). Later, patch-clamp recordings showed the currents through single Na+ channels, and the channels themselves were cloned and their structures solved.
  • Evaluate. Several independent methods agree, which makes the evidence strong. But not every action potential depends on Na+: the upstroke in the cells of the sinoatrial node is carried by Ca2+, and repolarization depends on K+. The sodium pump isn’t directly involved, but the gradient it maintains is essential in the long run.

questions.title: Chemical transmission at the neuromuscular junction
questions.text: What is the evidence that transmission between nerve and muscle is chemical in nature?
questions.guidance:
Some points to consider. This isn’t a model answer.

  • A junction that drugs act on. In the 1850s Claude Bernard found that curare stopped stimulation of the nerve from making the muscle contract, although the nerve still conducted, and the muscle still contracted when it was stimulated directly. So curare acts at the junction between them, and Langley later proposed a “receptive substance” there.
  • The transmitter. Loewi (1921) showed that the vagus nerve slows the heart by releasing a substance that can slow a second heart, later identified as acetylcholine. Dale, Feldberg and Vogt (1936) collected acetylcholine from muscles when their motor nerves were stimulated (with an anticholinesterase to stop it being broken down), and acetylcholine injected close to a muscle made it contract.
  • The end-plate potential. Recorded close to the junction, it’s local and graded, it dies away with distance, and tubocurarine reduces it until the muscle no longer reaches threshold (Fatt and Katz, 1951). Anticholinesterases make it larger and longer. There’s also a synaptic delay of about half a millisecond, too long for current simply flowing from nerve to muscle.
  • Quanta. Miniature end-plate potentials appear even when the nerve isn’t stimulated (Fatt and Katz, 1952). Curare blocks them and anticholinesterases prolong them, so they’re caused by acetylcholine released in packets, and the end-plate potential is built from many of them (del Castillo and Katz, 1954). Electron microscopy then showed the vesicles, and release turned out to depend on Ca2+ entering the terminal.
  • Toxins. Botulinum toxin stops vesicles fusing, α-latrotoxin makes them release their contents all at once, and tubocurarine blocks the receptors. Each fits a chemical mechanism, and none would make sense for an electrical one.
  • Why not electrical? The synaptic cleft is about 50 nm wide, with no gap junctions across it, and a small nerve terminal couldn’t pass enough current to depolarize a large muscle fibre directly.
  • Evaluate. Electrical synapses do exist elsewhere, through gap junctions, so it’s worth saying what chemical transmission gains here: amplification, one-way transmission and reliability, at the cost of a delay and of being open to drugs and toxins.

questions.title: The autonomic nervous system and drugs
questions.text: How can a knowledge of the autonomic nervous system be pharmacologically valuable?
questions.guidance:
Some points to consider. This isn’t a model answer.

  • Each step is a target. Knowing the transmitters and receptors, and how each transmitter is made, stored, released and removed, tells you where drugs can act and what to expect when they do.
  • The ganglia. Both divisions use acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors in their ganglia, a different type from those at the neuromuscular junction. Ganglion blockers such as hexamethonium were once used to lower blood pressure, but because they block both divisions they had many side effects, from a dry mouth and constipation to fainting on standing. That shows why selectivity matters.
  • The parasympathetic side. Muscarinic antagonists include atropine, which speeds a slow heart, dries secretions before surgery, and treats poisoning by organophosphates and nerve agents, which inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Tropicamide dilates the pupil for an eye examination, and ipratropium and tiotropium are inhaled to open the airways. Muscarinic agonists such as pilocarpine treat glaucoma.
  • The sympathetic side. β1-selective blockers such as atenolol slow the heart and lower blood pressure, while non-selective ones such as propranolol can make asthma worse by blocking the β2 receptors of the airways. β2 agonists such as salbutamol relieve asthma. Adrenaline treats anaphylaxis, and α1 agonists such as phenylephrine are used as decongestants.
  • Ending the signal. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of noradrenaline, and anticholinesterases prolong the action of acetylcholine. Sildenafil inhibits phosphodiesterase type 5, which prolongs the effect of nitric oxide.
  • Predicting effects. Knowing which division dominates a tissue predicts what a drug does there. A ganglion blocker speeds the heart, because vagal tone dominates at rest, but dilates blood vessels, which are mainly under sympathetic control. And adrenaline has different effects at different concentrations: at low ones it relaxes the vessels of skeletal muscle through β2 receptors, and at high ones it constricts them through α receptors.
  • Evaluate. The value is in the details. The two divisions aren’t simply equal and opposite, so a drug’s effects depend on the tissue, the receptor subtype and the dose, and its side effects come from the same receptors in other tissues.
